title: Clerk Threw Grandma OUT, Unaware She Came to Spend $10,000

scenes.text: Sweetheart, in December of two thousand nine, a young clerk at the fanciest department store in Columbus looked at my old coat and my snow boots, and she told me to leave, because the store was for customers. What she didn't know was that I had a check in my purse for ten thousand dollars, and I'd come to spend every penny of it, that day, in her department.
scenes.query: elderly woman in old coat at fancy store
scenes.caption: THIS STORE IS FOR CUSTOMERS

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you where that check came from, what I said to that clerk, and what happened when the store manager came running down the escalator. Stay with me, honey, because the ending isn't about getting even. It's about what that young woman did three weeks later, and it made me cry in the middle of a church.
scenes.caption: THE MANAGER CAME RUNNING

scenes.text: Every winter at our church, we had a coat drive for the children at Lincoln Elementary, the poorest school in Mansfield. People would bring in their old coats, and we'd wash them and mend them and hand them out. But that year, the coats coming in were thin and worn out, honey. And I saw a little boy at the bus stop in December wearing a summer windbreaker and two sweatshirts underneath.
scenes.query: child at bus stop in thin jacket snow
scenes.caption: A SUMMER WINDBREAKER

scenes.text: I went home and couldn't sleep. So I went to the church council and said, this year, let's buy them new coats. Real winter coats, brand new, with tags. Every child at Lincoln who needs one. The council laughed. They said, Ruth, there are a hundred and forty children at that school. Where are we going to get that kind of money? And I said, give me six weeks.
scenes.caption: GIVE ME SIX WEEKS

scenes.text: For six weeks, I baked. Every single day. Pies, cookies, cinnamon rolls, my mother's fruit bread. I sold them after church, at the hardware store, at the hospital, at the bowling alley. The ladies from my Bible study baked too. Then the newspaper wrote a little story about it, and the checks started coming. In a minute I'll tell you how much we raised. We were shocked.
scenes.query: table of pies and baked goods for sale
scenes.caption: SIX WEEKS OF BAKING

scenes.text: Ten thousand two hundred dollars, sweetheart. From pies and cookies and a little story in the paper. Enough for a hundred and forty good winter coats, with hats and mittens. The church treasurer wrote me a check, and I called the department store in Columbus that had the best children's coats, and they said to come on Saturday and their children's department would help me.
scenes.caption: TEN THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED

scenes.text: Now, on that Saturday, I'd been up since four in the morning baking the last order of pies. I was tired, honey. I didn't think about what I was wearing. My old brown car coat from the nineteen eighties, the one with the patch on the elbow. My snow boots with the salt stains. My hair under a plastic rain bonnet, because it was sleeting. I looked like what I was. A tired grandmother from Mansfield.
scenes.query: elderly woman in old brown coat rain bonnet
scenes.caption: A TIRED GRANDMOTHER

scenes.text: If you're enjoying Grandma's story, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. The children's department was on the third floor. It was beautiful. Christmas trees, music, little velvet coats on little mannequins. And behind the counter was a young woman, maybe twenty-two, very pretty, with long red nails, talking on her cell phone.
scenes.query: young clerk with red nails on phone
scenes.caption: LONG RED NAILS

scenes.text: I waited. And waited. Five minutes. Ten. She kept talking. Other customers came, in nice coats with shopping bags, and she hung up and helped them right away. Then she went back to her phone. Finally I said, excuse me, miss, I'm here to buy some children's coats. And she looked at me, up and down, from the rain bonnet to the salt-stained boots, and she sighed.
scenes.query: clerk looking woman up and down
scenes.caption: UP AND DOWN

scenes.text: She said, ma'am, the clearance rack is in the basement. These coats start at sixty dollars. I said, I know, dear. I'd like to buy a lot of them. And she laughed. She actually laughed, and said, ma'am, we don't do layaway. And then she leaned over the counter and said, a little louder, honestly, this floor is for customers. You're making people uncomfortable. Maybe you should go.
scenes.caption: YOU SHOULD GO

scenes.text: Everybody heard her, honey. A woman with a stroller stared at me. A man looked away. I felt my face get hot all the way to my ears. For one second, I was ten years old again on Elm Street, in a hand-me-down coat, and the rich girls were laughing. I almost left. I almost turned around and walked right out. And then I thought about that little boy in the windbreaker.
scenes.caption: I ALMOST LEFT

scenes.text: And I'll tell you something, sweetheart. I've been on both sides of that counter. When I was sixteen, I worked at the Woolworth's on Main Street, and I saw how the girls treated the farm women who came in with mud on their boots and cash in a coffee can. Those farm women always had the cash. The ladies in the fur coats were the ones who bought on credit and never paid.
scenes.caption: THE COFFEE CAN

scenes.text: So I didn't leave. I opened my purse, very slowly, and I took out that check, and I laid it flat on her glass counter, right in front of her red nails. Ten thousand two hundred dollars, made out to the store. And I said, quietly, dear, I'd like a hundred and forty winter coats, in children's sizes four through twelve. With hats and mittens. And I'd like to pay today.
scenes.caption: A HUNDRED AND FORTY COATS

scenes.text: She looked at that check for a long time. She read it twice. Her face went white, and then pink, and then white again. She said, is this real? And I said, it's real, honey. It's pies. Six weeks of pies. And she picked up her phone, with her hand shaking, and called the manager. And I heard her whisper, I think I made a mistake.
scenes.caption: I MADE A MISTAKE

scenes.text: The manager came running down the escalator two steps at a time. A man in a gray suit, maybe fifty, out of breath. He'd talked to me on the phone that week. He said, Mrs. Miller? The coat lady from Mansfield? I read about you in the paper. And he shook my hand with both of his and said, welcome, welcome. Right in front of that clerk, and the woman with the stroller, and everybody.
scenes.caption: THE COAT LADY

scenes.text: So far, the windbreaker, the pies, the counter, and the check. Then the manager turned to that clerk and said, Ashley, you're done for today. Go to my office. And she started to cry, right there. And here's the part people don't expect, honey. I said, no. Please. I'd like Ashley to help me. I'd like her to pick out every single coat with me. All hundred and forty.
scenes.caption: ASHLEY WILL HELP ME

scenes.text: The manager looked at me like I was crazy. Ashley looked at me like I was crazy. But I said, Ashley, I want you to see who these coats are for. And so for three hours, that girl and I went through every rack. I told her about the boy in the windbreaker. About the girl who wore her mother's coat down to her ankles. About the twins who shared one coat and took turns going to school.
scenes.query: two women choosing children's coats on racks
scenes.caption: WHO THE COATS ARE FOR

scenes.text: Somewhere around coat number sixty, honey, Ashley stopped talking on her phone. Around coat number ninety, she started asking questions. Is the little girl's favorite color purple? Does the boy need a big size, so it lasts two winters? And around coat number one hundred and twenty, she told me she'd grown up in a trailer in southern Ohio, and her mother had bought her coats at the Goodwill.
scenes.query: young woman holding purple child's coat
scenes.caption: SHE GREW UP POOR

scenes.text: She said, Mrs. Miller, I'm so ashamed. When I saw your coat and your boots, I saw my mother. And I've spent five years trying to get as far away from my mother as I can. I got this job, and these nails, and these clothes, so nobody would ever look at me the way people used to look at us. And then I looked at you exactly that way. I'm so sorry.
scenes.caption: I SAW MY MOTHER

scenes.text: I took her hands, red nails and all, and I said, honey, I know. I know that feeling better than you think. But the way out of being looked down on isn't to look down on somebody else. It's to look up. And she cried, and I cried, and the manager brought us both coffee and pretended he wasn't crying, too. We finished at five o'clock.
scenes.query: elderly woman holding young woman's hands
scenes.caption: LOOK UP

scenes.text: The manager gave us twenty percent off. Then he took another hundred dollars out of his own wallet. And with the money we saved, we bought thirty more coats, honey. A hundred and seventy coats, in a moving truck the store paid for, delivered to Lincoln Elementary on the Monday before Christmas break.
scenes.query: moving truck full of coats at school
scenes.caption: A HUNDRED AND SEVENTY COATS

scenes.text: And then the part I promised you. The Sunday after Christmas, I was sitting in my pew at church, and the door opened at the back, and in walked Ashley. No red nails. No designer coat. And with her was a little woman in a worn Goodwill coat. Her mother. They'd driven two hours from southern Ohio. Ashley walked her mother right down the aisle and sat her next to me.
scenes.query: young woman bringing mother into church
scenes.caption: SHE BROUGHT HER MOTHER

scenes.text: After the service, Ashley handed the minister an envelope. She'd been saving all month. Three hundred dollars, honey, from a girl making nine dollars an hour. For next year's coats. And she said, I want to help you bake. Every Saturday next fall. If you'll teach me. And I said, honey, I'll teach you my mother's fruit bread, and I've never taught that to anybody.
scenes.caption: TEACH ME TO BAKE

scenes.text: Ashley's been baking with me every fall for sixteen years, sweetheart. She runs the whole coat drive now. Last winter, we bought four hundred coats for three different schools. She's a manager at that same store, and every new clerk she trains gets the same speech. She tells them about the old lady in the rain bonnet. And she tells them, you never know who's standing at your counter.
scenes.caption: YOU NEVER KNOW

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, honey. When somebody treats you badly, you can walk out, or you can make them sorry. Or there's a third way. You can make them part of something good. It's the hardest of the three. But it's the only one that changes anything. And it's the one my mother would have chosen.
scenes.query: children in new winter coats in snow
scenes.caption: THE THIRD WAY

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Would you have stayed and let Ashley help, or would you have walked out? Be honest with Grandma. There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next one. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WOULD YOU HAVE STAYED?
